overview:
Avadhi-jnana (Sanskrit: अवधिज्ञान, avadhijñāna; Prakrit: ओहिणाण, ohināṇa) is one of the five principal modes of knowledge recognized in Jain epistemology, alongside mati-jnana (sensory-cognitive knowledge), shruta-jnana (scriptural knowledge), manahparyaya-jnana (telepathic knowledge), and kevala-jnana (omniscience). It is usually translated as “clairvoyant knowledge” or “clairvoyance,” but in the Jain context it has a precise technical meaning: a direct, extra-sensory cognition of material objects that is limited in scope by substance (dravya), space (kshetra), time (kala), and modes (bhava).

Unlike ordinary sense-based knowing, avadhi-jnana does not depend on the external senses or the mind as instruments. It is a form of immediate, non-discursive awareness arising from the soul itself when certain knowledge-obscuring karmas (jnanavaraniya) are partially destroyed or suppressed. The objects of avadhi-jnana are always corporeal or formed entities; Jain texts emphasize that it does not grasp formless realities such as pure souls or abstract categories. Within its domain, however, it can extend across great distances of space and time, and can penetrate obstacles that would block ordinary perception.

Classical Jain works describe avadhi-jnana as “limited” in contrast to kevala-jnana. The limitation is fourfold: in terms of the number and kind of substances known, the spatial range, the temporal span (past and future), and the variety of modes or states of those substances. For example, a being endowed with avadhi-jnana may intuit innumerable corporeal objects, innumerable regions of space, or innumerable moments of time, yet still not know all possible modes of all substances. This finitude is essential to its definition and marks it as an intermediate stage on the path toward omniscience.

From the standpoint of karmic causation, Jain doctrine distinguishes between avadhi-jnana that arises naturally by birth (bhava-pratyaya avadhi) and avadhi-jnana that is acquired through spiritual effort (guna-pratyaya or kshayopashamika avadhi). The first type is said to be innate in celestial beings (devas) and hell-inhabitants (narakis), who possess it as a consequence of their particular destinies. The second type can be attained by humans and certain animals through the destruction-cum-subsidence (kshayopashama) of the specific avadhijnanavaraniya (clairvoyant-knowledge-obscuring) karmas, often in conjunction with austerities, vows, and purification of conduct.

Within guna-pratyaya avadhi, texts such as the Tattvartha-sutra and its commentaries describe several sub-classifications. Deśāvadhi-jnana (limited clairvoyance) is knowledge restricted by substance, space, time, or modes and is further divided into types that increase, decrease, remain steady, or fluctuate, and that may or may not continue across births or regions. More expansive forms such as paramāvadhi-jnana (supreme clairvoyance) and sarvāvadhi-jnana (complete clairvoyance) are associated with highly advanced ascetics nearing kevala-jnana, whose clairvoyant range extends to countless regions of the universe and approaches knowledge of all knowables.

In the canonical and post-canonical literature, avadhi-jnana is treated both as a doctrinal category and as a lived spiritual capacity. It is “right” (samyag-avadhi) only when accompanied by right faith (samyag-darshana); otherwise, it can be perverted or mixed with wrong belief. As a mode of right knowledge (samyag-jnana), it contributes to the triad of right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct that leads toward liberation (moksha). At the same time, Jain authors warn that the mere possession of extraordinary cognition does not guarantee ethical purity or final release, since karmic bondage can persist even in beings with remarkable clairvoyant powers.

Avadhi-jnana also plays a role in the technical analysis of karma. The avadhijnanavaraniya karma is one of the five divisions of the jnanavaraniya (knowledge-obscuring) karmas, and its subsidence or destruction is the specific condition for the arising of clairvoyant knowledge. As the soul progresses through the gunasthanas (spiritual stages), the refinement and expansion of avadhi-jnana can mark important thresholds, especially in the higher stages where paramāvadhi and sarvāvadhi forms appear. Yet, in all cases, avadhi-jnana remains a conditioned, partial knowledge that points beyond itself to the unconditioned omniscience of kevala-jnana.

Across both Digambara and Svetambara traditions, the basic structure of avadhi-jnana as extra-sensory, materially focused, and karmically conditioned is shared, though individual texts may differ in the details of classification and terminology. Modern scholarship often compares Jain avadhi-jnana with notions of clairvoyance or mystic vision in other traditions, but the Jain framework insists on its integration into a rigorous metaphysics of substances, space, time, and modes, and a precise doctrine of karmic causality. In this way, avadhi-jnana is not merely a curiosity of paranormal experience but a carefully theorized stage in the soul’s journey from limited knowing to omniscience.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra (also Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (traditionally)
primary_sources.translation:
“Avadhi (clairvoyant knowledge) arising from destiny (bhava-pratyaya) belongs to the gods and hell-inhabitants.
For the remaining beings, it (avadhi) is of six varieties, caused by destruction-cum-subsidence (of the relevant karmas).”
primary_sources.notes: These sutras occur in the first chapter of the Tattvārtha-sūtra, in the section on the types of knowledge (jñāna). The text distinguishes avadhi-jnana based on its causal conditions: naturally arising in celestial and hellish beings, and arising through kṣayopaśama of avadhijnanavaraniya karma in humans and animals. Commentarial traditions elaborate the sixfold division of deśāvadhi-jnana (limited clairvoyance) and further higher forms such as paramāvadhi and sarvāvadhi.

primary_sources.title: Nandī-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed within the Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text: मति श्रुत अवधि मनःपर्यय केवलं ति पञ्च विण्णाणाणि ।
primary_sources.transliteration: mati śruta avadhi manaḥparyaya kevalaṃ ti pañca viṇṇāṇāṇi.
primary_sources.translation: “Mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyaya, and kevala—these are the five kinds of knowledge.”
primary_sources.notes: The Nandī-sūtra is a canonical Śvetāmbara text devoted to the analysis of cognition and knowledge. In its enumeration of the five types of jñāna, avadhi-jnana is listed as the third, following sensory-cognitive (mati) and scriptural (śruta) knowledge, and preceding telepathic (manaḥparyaya) and omniscient (kevala) knowledge. Subsequent sections discuss the characteristics and subdivisions of each type, situating avadhi-jnana within a broader epistemological framework.

primary_sources.title: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra (Lives of the Sixty-Three Illustrious Persons)
primary_sources.author: Hemacandra
primary_sources.original_text: अवधिज्ञानं देवानां नरकिणां च स्वभावजं । अन्येषां तु षड्विधं क्षयोपशमलक्षणम् ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
avadhijñānaṃ devānāṃ narakiṇāṃ ca svabhāvajaṃ.
anyeṣāṃ tu ṣaḍ-vidhaṃ kṣayopaśama-lakṣaṇam.
primary_sources.translation:
“Avadhi-knowledge is innate by nature in the gods and hell-inhabitants.
For the others, it is sixfold, characterized by destruction-and-subsidence (of karmas).”
primary_sources.notes: Hemacandra’s epic, while narrative in form, incorporates doctrinal passages summarizing Jain teachings. In the context of Ṛṣabha’s sermon on right knowledge, avadhi-jnana is described as a mode of samyag-jnana (right knowledge) and its distribution among different classes of beings is outlined. The passage reflects and popularizes the technical doctrine found in the Tattvārtha-sūtra and related texts.

misconceptions.myth: Avadhi-jnana is the same as omniscience (kevala-jnana) and knows everything without limitation.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine explicitly defines avadhi-jnana as limited knowledge. It is constrained by substance, space, time, and modes, and its objects are only corporeal entities. Kevala-jnana alone is unlimited, all-encompassing omniscience; avadhi-jnana is an intermediate, partial stage on the path toward that goal.

misconceptions.myth: Avadhi-jnana can know formless souls and abstract realities just like physical objects.
misconceptions.reality: Canonical descriptions emphasize that avadhi-jnana has material objects as its domain. It cognizes things with shape or form and does not directly grasp formless substances such as pure souls or purely abstract categories. Knowledge of such realities belongs to higher modes, especially kevala-jnana.

misconceptions.myth: Any spiritually inclined person can easily develop avadhi-jnana through simple practices.
misconceptions.reality: Avadhi-jnana arises only under specific karmic conditions. In many beings it is present by birth (bhava-pratyaya) due to particular destinies, while in humans and certain animals it requires the destruction-cum-subsidence of avadhijnanavaraniya karmas, often at advanced stages of spiritual development. Jain texts treat it as rare and significant, not as a routine or easily acquired ability.

misconceptions.myth: Avadhi-jnana is merely a poetic or symbolic way of talking about strong intuition or imagination.
misconceptions.reality: Within the Jain philosophical system, avadhi-jnana is a rigorously defined epistemic category. It is distinguished from sense-based cognition, scriptural learning, and mental constructs, and is tied to precise karmic mechanisms and classifications. While modern readers may compare it to ideas of clairvoyance or mystic vision, Jain authors treat it as a real, extra-sensory mode of knowing with specific doctrinal functions.
